title: What is EC2, what are instance families/types (general purpose, compute/memory/storage optimized), and what parameters do you consider when launching an instance (AMI, instance type, key pair, security group, subnet, IAM role, storage)?
shortTitle: EC2, Instance Families and Launch Parameters

s1_definition.profdef: EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is the AWS service that provides resizable virtual servers on demand. Instance families group instance types by the resource profile they optimize: general purpose (balanced CPU and memory, the M and T families), compute optimized (high CPU, the C family), memory optimized (large RAM, the R and X families), and storage optimized (high local disk throughput, the I and D families). When launching an instance you choose an AMI (the disk image), an instance type (the size and family), a key pair (for SSH), one or more security groups (the firewall), a subnet (the network placement), an IAM role (its AWS permissions), and storage (EBS volumes).
s1_definition.analogy: EC2 is renting an office room from National Bank of India's building instead of constructing your own. The instance family is the type of room: a general-purpose desk, a powerful number-crunching room for the compute team, a huge room full of filing cabinets for memory-heavy work, or a room with fast delivery chutes for storage-heavy work. When you rent the room you pick its layout (AMI), its size (instance type), the key to its door (key pair), the security guard rules (security group), which floor it sits on (subnet), its clearance badge (IAM role), and its cabinets (storage).
s1_definition.oneliner: EC2 is a rented virtual server, the family picks what it is good at, and launching it means choosing its image, size, key, firewall, network, permissions, and disks.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud) is the AWS service that provides resizable virtual servers on demand. Instance families group instance types by the resource profile they optimize: general purpose (balanced CPU and memory, the M and T families), compute optimized (high CPU, the C family), memory optimized (large RAM, the R and X families), and storage optimized (high local disk throughput, the I and D families). When launching an instance you choose an AMI (the disk image), an instance type (the size and family), a key pair (for SSH), one or more security groups (the firewall), a subnet (the network placement), an IAM role (its AWS permissions), and storage (EBS volumes).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** EC2 is renting an office room from National Bank of India's building instead of constructing your own. The instance family is the type of room: a general-purpose desk, a powerful number-crunching room for the compute team, a huge room full of filing cabinets for memory-heavy work, or a room with fast delivery chutes for storage-heavy work. When you rent the room you pick its layout (AMI), its size (instance type), the key to its door (key pair), the security guard rules (security group), which floor it sits on (subnet), its clearance badge (IAM role), and its cabinets (storage).

**One line to remember:** EC2 is a rented virtual server, the family picks what it is good at, and launching it means choosing its image, size, key, firewall, network, permissions, and disks.

sections.s2_technical:
EC2 gives you a virtual machine in minutes. You never see the physical hardware; AWS runs a hypervisor and carves out your instance. You pay per second or hour while it runs, and you can stop or terminate it when done.

Instance families match the workload. General purpose M-family instances suit our typical banking web and API services where CPU and memory are balanced. The T family is burstable — cheap for workloads that are idle most of the time and spike occasionally, like an internal admin tool. Compute optimized C-family instances suit CPU-heavy work such as risk calculations or fraud-model scoring. Memory optimized R and X family instances suit in-memory caches and large JVM heaps, like a market-data service holding millions of quotes. Storage optimized I and D family instances suit databases needing very fast local disks.

The launch parameters each have a purpose. The AMI (Amazon Machine Image) is the starting disk — the operating system plus any pre-baked software, for example an Amazon Linux image with Java 17 already installed. The instance type is the family and size, like `m6i.large`. The key pair is the SSH key used to log into a Linux instance. The security group is a stateful firewall controlling inbound and outbound traffic. The subnet determines which VPC and Availability Zone the instance lives in and whether it is public or private. The IAM role (via an instance profile) gives the instance temporary credentials to call AWS services without embedded keys. The storage is EBS volumes — the root volume plus any extra data volumes.

```java
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.ec2.Ec2Client;
import software.amazon.awssdk.services.ec2.model.*;

Ec2Client ec2 = Ec2Client.create();
RunInstancesRequest req = RunInstancesRequest.builder()
        .imageId("ami-0abcd1234")              // AMI: Amazon Linux + Java 17
        .instanceType(InstanceType.M6I_LARGE)  // general purpose, balanced
        .keyName("nbi-settlement-key")         // SSH key pair
        .securityGroupIds("sg-0settlement")    // firewall
        .subnetId("subnet-0private-a")         // private subnet, AZ a
        .iamInstanceProfile(IamInstanceProfileSpecification.builder()
                .name("SettlementReaderProfile").build())  // IAM role, no keys
        .minCount(1).maxCount(1)
        .build();
ec2.runInstances(req);
```

A senior nuance: choosing the right size is a cost and performance decision. Over-provisioning wastes money, under-provisioning causes throttling. We use CloudWatch metrics and AWS Compute Optimizer to right-size, and we prefer the latest generation (the `6i`/`7g` suffixes) because newer hardware is cheaper per unit of performance. Graviton (ARM, the `g` suffix) is often cheapest for JVM workloads.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs a fraud-scoring service that is CPU-heavy and a market-data cache that is memory-heavy. Putting both on the same general-purpose instance means one starves the other and we pay for the wrong resource. This is exactly what instance families solve: pick a compute-optimized type for fraud scoring and a memory-optimized type for the cache.

Problem 2 — Every launch must specify the full set of parameters correctly, or the instance is insecure or unreachable. A missing IAM role forces embedded keys; a wrong subnet makes it unreachable; a wrong security group blocks SSH. This is exactly why we model a launch specification and validate it before launching.

We will build an `InstanceLauncher` that validates and records a launch specification, plus an `InstanceTypeAdvisor` that recommends a family for a workload. Classes: `LaunchSpec`, `InstanceTypeAdvisor`, `InstanceLauncher`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two workload profiles (fraud scoring is CPU-heavy, market-data cache is memory-heavy) and a full launch specification.

Step 1 — The `InstanceTypeAdvisor` maps the fraud-scoring profile `cpu-heavy` to `c6i.2xlarge`, a compute-optimized type, and the cache profile `memory-heavy` to `r6i.2xlarge`, a memory-optimized type. Choosing the right family means we pay for the resource the workload actually consumes.

Step 2 — A `LaunchSpec` is assembled for the fraud service: the AMI (Amazon Linux with Java), the recommended compute type, the SSH key pair, the security group, a private subnet in Availability Zone a, the IAM instance profile, and a fifty-gigabyte root volume.

Step 3 — The `InstanceLauncher` validates the spec. It refuses if the AMI is missing, if there is no IAM role (which would force embedded keys), or if there is no security group. All are present, so validation passes.

Step 4 — The launcher returns an instance ID, standing in for the real `runInstances` call. The instance boots from the AMI into the private subnet with its firewall and its role-based credentials.

```
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Fraud scoring recommended type: c6i.2xlarge
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Market-data cache recommended type: r6i.2xlarge
2026-10-29 00:52:14 [INFO] Launched instance i-1a2b3c4d with spec c6i.2xlarge in subnet-0private-a role=SettlementReaderProfile disk=50GB
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Workload profile ──→ InstanceTypeAdvisor.recommend()
    │ cpu-heavy    → c6i.2xlarge (compute optimized)
    │ memory-heavy → r6i.2xlarge (memory optimized)
    ▼
  LaunchSpec { AMI, type, keyPair, SG, subnet, IAM profile, disk }
    │
    ▼
  InstanceLauncher.launch(spec)
    │ validate AMI, IAM role, security group ── missing → reject
    │ all present
    ▼
  EC2 runInstances → instance boots in private subnet (AZ-a)
    with role credentials + firewall + EBS root volume
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
EC2 is Amazon's service for renting resizable virtual servers on demand. Instead of buying hardware and waiting weeks, I call an API and get a running machine in minutes, paying per second while it runs. The thing that matters most when picking an instance is the family, because each family optimizes a different resource. General purpose M and T families balance CPU and memory and suit typical web and API services, compute optimized C family suits CPU-heavy work like risk and fraud scoring, memory optimized R and X families suit large in-memory caches and big JVM heaps, and storage optimized I and D families suit databases that need very fast local disks.

When I launch an instance I think through seven parameters, each with a clear job. The AMI is the starting disk image — the operating system plus any pre-installed software like Java. The instance type is the family and size together, such as m6i.large. The key pair is the SSH key I use to log into a Linux box. The security group is the stateful firewall that controls inbound and outbound traffic. The subnet decides which VPC and Availability Zone the instance sits in and whether it is public or private. The IAM role, attached through an instance profile, gives the instance temporary credentials to call AWS services so I never embed access keys. And the storage is the EBS volumes — the root volume plus any extra data disks.

At National Bank of India I used this directly. Our fraud-scoring service is CPU-heavy, so it runs on a compute-optimized C-family type, while our market-data cache is memory-heavy, so it runs on a memory-optimized R-family type. Matching the family to the workload means we pay for the resource the service actually consumes instead of starving one and wasting the other. Every launch goes into a private subnet with a tight security group and an IAM instance profile, so there are no embedded keys and nothing is exposed to the internet.

One senior point I always add is right-sizing and generation choice. Over-provisioning wastes money and under-provisioning causes throttling, so I use CloudWatch metrics and AWS Compute Optimizer to pick the right size, and I prefer the latest generation because newer hardware is cheaper per unit of performance. For JVM workloads I often choose Graviton, the ARM-based g-suffix types, because they usually give the best price for performance, which is exactly the kind of cost discipline a bank expects.

keyPoints: EC2: virtual servers in the cloud
Instance types: General (T3), Compute (C5), Memory (R5), GPU (P3)
